_comment: WHAT THIS CAR IS LIKE.
A normal line pool, deliberately — `car_character` needs no new code and
no new data format, because `lines.allowed()` already gates on exactly
the things that decide whether a sentence about a car is true:
"disc":  ["f1"]           discipline
"era":   ["turbo", "v10"] period
"year":  [1988, 1988]      an exact season, where it matters
"needs": ["ers"]          the car actually HAS the thing
"not":   ["drs"]          ...and does not have this one
That is why this file covers a Group C car and a Super Touring saloon and
a Next Gen Cup car, not just the three seasons the driver knowledge base
holds. A one-off race for fun gets real colour about the machinery, which
is the whole point of the layer.
TWO RULES, BOTH LEARNED ELSEWHERE IN THIS PROJECT:
1. CAPABILITY, NOT OUTCOME. Say what these cars DO — the boost limit, the
fuel ration, how they follow in traffic. Never what happened in the
real season: the booth is presenting a race the user is driving, and
'McLaren won fifteen of sixteen that year' both spoils it and is
contradicted by the timing screen. The archive rules in
booth_archive.json say the same thing and flowtest.py checks them.
2. NOBODY IN THIS BOOTH DROVE THESE CARS. Chuck is a NASCAR Cup champion
and Brett a WEC champion; neither has sat in a Formula One car. Lines
here are third person or use the general 'you', never 'when I drove
one of these'. eratest.py greps for the first-person form.
Delivered as filler, one per session per fact, sharing the driver-fact
family gate — a booth that alternates driver trivia and car trivia every
thirty seconds is a documentary, not a broadcast.

car_character.t: Unlimited boost for one lap in qualifying, and well over a thousand horsepower with it. The chassis never really expected that.
Turbo lag you could measure in corners. Get on the throttle where you want the power and you are already late.
A hundred and fifty litres for the whole race and no refuelling. These drivers are turning the boost down and saving fuel while they race each other.
The boost is capped this year and the fuel is rationed, so a turbo car cannot simply be driven flat out. Run it hard early and you will not see the flag.
This is the last season turbos are allowed at all, and the rules have been written to make them uncomfortable. Half this field has already given up on them.
Two kinds of car out here. The turbos have the power and a fuel limit to worry about; the naturally aspirated cars have neither.
Manual gearbox, no power steering, and enough power to spin the wheels in fourth. These asked a lot.
Three and a half litres, no turbo, and a V10 that wants to be at the top of the rev range all afternoon.
Refuelling is back in this era, so the strategy is a real weapon again.
Active suspension, traction control, semi-automatic gearboxes — the electronics peaked here and then the rules took them away.
Grooved tyres and a narrow track. It looks fast and it is genuinely harder work than it looks.
Carbon brakes, a sequential box and an engine screaming past fifteen thousand. The noise alone tells you what era this is.
The aerodynamics are getting serious now, but the driver is still doing all the difficult parts himself.
A one-point-six litre V6, two electric motors and about a thousand horsepower between them. These are the most complicated racing cars ever built.
The fuel flow is capped, so the engine cannot simply be turned up. Everything is about how the energy gets used.
Deployment and harvesting — where a driver spends his battery around a lap is a lap time in itself.
This is the last year of these regulations, and the cars are as developed as they are ever going to be.
Two different design philosophies on this grid — one lot running the car nose-down and flat, the other raking it up at the back. They are quick in different corners.
The floor rules were trimmed for this season and it cost some cars more than others. Not everybody arrived here with the same car they finished last year with.
Ground effect. The downforce comes from underneath the car now, and that is why they can follow each other like this.
These run the floor low and stiff, so ride height is everything. Get it wrong over a kerb and the car does the rest.
Eighteen-inch wheels, and the best part of eight hundred kilos before it takes on any fuel. They are heavy cars, and you see it on the brakes.
Racing got closer when the aerodynamics moved under the floor. Whatever else you say about these rules, they did that.
Cigar-shaped, skinny tyres, and downforce nobody had invented yet. It is all mechanical grip and bravery.
No seatbelt worth the name and no run-off to speak of. A different sport, and not only in the lap times.
Wings arrived and nobody was quite sure how strong to build them. These cars are a live experiment.
Slicks and wings and a Cosworth in the back — half this grid is running the same engine as the other half.
A works team and a private entry could buy the same engine in this era, and that is why the grids were so big.
The tyres go off and there is nothing to do about it but drive around the problem.
Balance of performance, so the field is levelled on paper. What is left is the driving and the pit wall.
ABS and traction control on these, which sounds like a shortcut and is not — it moves the difficulty somewhere else.
A GT car is a road car underneath, and it never quite lets you forget it. Weight transfer everywhere.
The pit window is a strategy in itself here. Nobody wins one of these on outright pace alone.
Traffic is the enemy in this kind of racing. Half the lap time is what you do about the car you are catching.
Headlights on, and the circuit changes completely. Braking points you have run all day suddenly need finding again.
Fuel allowance racing. There is a number of litres for the whole race and no way around it.
Closed cockpit, enormous downforce, and a top speed down the straights that belongs on a runway.
A hybrid front axle that only deploys above a certain speed. It is a rule that shapes how the corner exits look.
Two litres, no turbo, and a full works effort behind every one of them. Touring car racing was never cheap.
Contact is part of this discipline. The cars are built expecting it and the drivers race accordingly.
Heavy, powerful, and running on a set of tyres that will not last. Everything about this discipline is management.
The draft does half the driving for you out here, and it takes it back the moment you are on your own.
Restarts are where these races are decided. Everything before one is positioning.
Independent rear suspension, a sequential box and eighteen-inch wheels — this generation of Cup car drives nothing like the last one.
Push-to-pass. A fixed number of seconds of extra power for the whole race, and knowing when to spend it is the skill.
The same car races an oval one weekend and a street circuit the next. Nothing else in motorsport asks that.
No aids of any kind in this thing. Whatever the car does, the driver asked for it.
Compound choice is a real decision in this era — the softer tyre is quicker and it will not go the distance.
The aerodynamics on these are so sensitive that following closely destroys them. That is why the gaps stabilise.
